architecture.title: The NAT hotel agent inside an OpenShell sandbox on the Spark
architecture.caption: The gateway (a systemd user service running k3s in Docker) creates the sandbox from policies/hotel_agent_policy.yaml. Landlock confines writes to /sandbox and /tmp; the process runs as the unprivileged user 'sandbox'; every outbound connection goes through the egress proxy, which denies anything no policy group names (host + port + binary). The agent's model calls go to https://inference.local/v1, which the proxy routes to the provider local-vllm — vLLM on the Spark's host IP. Your laptop only runs the CLI and the offline policy labs.

sequence.title: Lab 15-4 — from policy file to a fenced agent (course-designed, not yet run on a Spark)
sequence.caption: Provider and inference routing are the playbook's Steps 6–7. The sandbox for a NAT agent is course-designed: NAT is installed while the setup-only pypi group is open, then the group is removed with a hot-reload before the agent runs. The last two steps are the proof: the model call is routed, a direct internet call is denied.

charts.title: Lab 15-3 — 13 agent actions against policies/hotel_agent_policy.yaml
charts.caption: From one run of lab 15-3 on this Mac, using policykit.decide — a course-made teaching model of OpenShell's policy semantics, not OpenShell. The 5 allows and 1 routed call are the agent doing its job (plus pip during setup); all 7 denies are the hijack attempts.

charts.title: Lab 15-2 — who catches which broken policy?
charts.caption: From one run of lab 15-2 on this Mac: 8 deliberately broken variants of the hotel policy. The real OpenShell 0.0.111 parser rejects the 3 structural mistakes (Version, list instead of map, unknown field `description`). policykit reports errors for those 3 plus the 3 semantic ones the gateway checks on push (relative path, root, missing port), and warnings for the 2 that apply but then deny every call (no binaries, no access mode).
